name: Dutch Sign Language
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Dutch Sign Language (dutc1253) is not in the catalog (the build carries it as not a distinct language / out of scope for a spoken-language word-stress catalog, with a Klomp 2021 grammar quote on sign-internal prominence already held by the project; this search of works with stress in the title produced a single title hit, Esteve-Gibert, Liszkowski & Prieto 2016 (Benjamins, doi:10.1075/ihll.6.12est), and it is a false positive: Glottolog record 514189 states its language code was a 'computerized assignment from \"pointing\"', and the abstract (saved from Crossref and the JBE landing page) concerns spoken child-directed speech prosody (intonation contour, pitch range, syllable duration) accompanying pointing gestures in nine caregiver-infant dyads — not NGT and not word stress. The chapter is paywalled with no open copy found (OpenAlex closed, no repository fulltext); priority none. No new first-hand stress statement for NGT was read in this search of works with stress in the title; nothing here changes the existing out-of-scope treatment.

new_statements.quote: As mentioned above, prosodic words need to have a least one stressed syllable. Which syllable receives stress is obvious for monosyllabic signs, but when it comes to polysyllabic signs, the pattern depends on the type of polysyllabic sign. Van der Kooij & Crasborn (2008) found that there are two types of polysyllabic signs in NGT, which show different strategies of emphasis. The first type consists of signs in which the first movement is repeated once or multiple times, such as the sign for RAIN (REGENEN, Figure 2.51). In this type, the first syllable is considered most prominent [...] The second type relates to signs in which the second movement is different from the first [...] In these cases, it is the second syllable that receives emphatic stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sign language (visual-manual modality): a syllable = one movement unit. Every prosodic word has at least one stressed syllable; monosyllabic signs are trivially stressed. In polysyllabic signs the stressed syllable is predictable from the sign's shape: if the sign repeats its first movement (e.g. RAIN), the first syllable is most prominent (articulated more strongly/sharply, optional emphatic head nod) and each following repetition is weaker ('fading out'); if the second movement differs from the first (opposite or perpendicular direction, e.g. POPE) the second syllable receives the emphatic stress (e.g. head nod). Compounds (e.g. FATHER^MOTHER 'parents') pattern with the second type, i.e. second-syllable stress. Realisation described in terms of emphasis rather than a positional stress grid.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. The foot level is described as understudied and its evidence in NGT 'scarce' (p. 134); a 'fading out' of successive repeated syllables is noted for the first type.
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the two-type split; compounds follow the second (second-syllable) type. Sentence-final copied pronoun is not stressed (p. 331, citing Bos 1995).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (prosodic word = single sign, or a lexical sign plus a cliticised light element such as a pointing sign). Based on van der Kooij & Crasborn 2008 (Lingua) with Corpus NGT examples; the statement is the grammar's own descriptive summary of that study.
new_statements.identity_note: Sign Language of the Netherlands / Nederlandse Gebarentaal (NGT), glottocode dutc1253, ISO 639-3 dse — a signed language, not a spoken one. 'Syllable' = movement unit and 'stress' = manual/non-manual emphasis of one movement (stronger, sharper articulation, head nod). Klomp 2021 describes the standard language as used in Corpus NGT; no regional variety is singled out. Note that Glottolog's descriptive bibliography for dutc1253 is polluted by automated keyword assignments from 'pointing' (Bejarano 2011, Floyd 2016, Cooperrider & Núñez 2012, Esteve-Gibert et al. 2016, etc.), none of which concern NGT.

sources.locator: pp. 138-139 (PDF page index 138-139 of 407; also p. 134 §2.1.2 Foot)
sources.note: Part 2 Phonology, Ch. 2 Prosody, §2.2.1 Prosodic word, pp. 138-139: every prosodic word has at least one stressed syllable; in polysyllabic signs stress depends on sign type — repeated-movement signs stress the first syllable (with fading out), signs whose second movement differs from the first, and compounds, stress the second syllable (citing van der Kooij & Crasborn 2008). §2.1.2 Foot (p. 134) notes the foot is understudied and evidence for it in NGT is scarce. §2.6.3 (p. 331): sentence-final copied pronoun is not stressed (Bos 1995).
